“#Prevent, #Engage and#Act”

These were the three keywords I brought back home from the ReAct Asia Pacific Regional Conference on#AMR 2026, held in Jakarta last week.
 
Just ahead of#WAAW2026, clinicians, researchers, policymakers, CSOs and youth came together for two days to deliberate on a collective course of action for the years ahead.

#Prevent: The updated WHO Global Action Plan (2026–2036) puts prevention first. As one speaker put it, infection control, immunisation and WASH are among the most powerful AMR programmes we have. That means stopping infections before they need #antibiotics. Another session suggested teaching infection prevention to students early, so they carry it into practice and pass it on to their peers.

#Engage: AMR can’t be fixed by the health sector alone. One participant asked where the ministers of agriculture and environment were in the room, and another said the finance minister should be involved from day zero. The session that stayed with me most put people at the centre. AMR survivor Ankita Mitra reminded us that an infection may be diagnosed in one person, but the consequences are lived by an entire family. Civil society, communities, and young people have to be part of the solution.

#Act: Plans are only as good as their delivery. Most plans are not costed, and WHO shared that only about 10% of countries had domestic funding for their national action plans in 2024. The call from the room was to cost the plan, set measurable indicators, close the reporting gap, and scale what already works.

My biggest learning was seemingly obvious: AMR cannot be tackled without addressing the systemic challenges that sit beneath it. Plans stay unfunded, sectors stay siloed, and accountability stays weak. Access to antibiotics and diagnostics remains unequal, and infection control and primary care are still stretched thin. Climate change, disasters and conflict make all of this worse, because every flood or crisis can become an AMR event.
 
Underneath all of it is social inequity. Those who are poorer, more displaced, and further from care are the ones who face the weakest infection control, the limited access to diagnostics, and the highest costs when treatment fails. That is why so many well-designed plans don’t deliver: they work best for those who already have access. AMR is not only a health problem. It is a development problem and a health-system problem, and it needs to be treated as both.

We enountered some of these stories through the #SochSamajhKe fellowship, whichSuperheroes Against Superbugs organized earlier this year in collabortion withYouth Ki Awaaz. Seeing them echoed in Jakarta was a strong motivation for us to continue our work at SaS.

Sarsha Braim read her job offer on a bathroom break, halfway through a waitressing shift.

Last month she was in Cannes for MIPCOM (her first time in France), selling sport content to TV broadcasters alongside studios like Paramount and Disney.

Not long before that offer, she'd finished uni, applied for a few jobs in sport and heard nothing back. She had about 10 LinkedIn connections, all from one uni class, and was convinced that "I'm not some big CEO, so no one wants to hear from me."

55 days after joining TheSportsGrad Method, she was approached for a job at Inverleigh, a sports media company she'd never heard of.

So what did she do differently?

She started posting about ice hockey, a sport she genuinely loves and that hardly anyone in Australia was writing about. Then every time someone liked or reacted to a post, she sent them a connection request within 24 hours, "while it's still fresh," so they'd remember her name.

One of those people was a co-founder of Inverleigh. He passed her name on to the company's commercial director, and the director messaged her about a job.

Posting on LinkedIn gets you seen, but the job comes from what you do after someone notices you. Think of a like as a wave from across the street: you can wave back and keep walking, or you can cross the road and say hello.

Today Sarsha is Commercial Partnerships Manager, Asia Pacific, flying to Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia to sell sport content to broadcasters.

If you want to try it this week:
1. Pick a sport you could post about for months (bonus points if hardly anyone else is covering it).
2. Post one thing you've noticed about it through the lens of the job you want. Partnerships? Break down a club's sponsors. Events? Review a match day. Analytics? Unpack one stat.
3. Set a 24-hour rule: everyone who reacts gets a connection request with a short note about the post.

Devo, I know, most of your posts will get a handful of likes and plenty of people won't accept. But you're not waiting on a job ad anymore, and you only need the right person to remember you.

My CV was rejected by a perfume brand. Not even invited for an interview, but it's ok :)

I have handled a local perfume brand before—from low awareness to shelf, from trial to repeat. And I have an obsession to build my own perfume brand. So I know the pain from the inside. 

What was in my head at that moment was this: "We need someone who can sell perfume in this crowded market".
My answer: "Everyone can sell perfume. Almost no one can make people REMEMBER perfume."

Look at their campaigns now: 15% - 35%++ discount in every campaign, and still low/not growing.

Discounts are not a strategy. It's a symptom.
A symptom that people try you once, and forget you tomorrow.

This is not a motivational post. This is my playbook.

IDR 10,884 BILLION — Indonesia fragrance market 2025, 8.4% CAGR
USD 361M → USD 635M by 2035

10 variants that all smell similar.
"Long-lasting 12 hours" + bottle photo + discount.
No hero. No story. No trial.
Result: Price war. No memory. No loyalty.

1. SELL IDENTITY, NOT NOTES
Notes "vanilla, musk, amber."
But "For women who want to be remembered when they leave the room."

2. ONE HERO, NOT 10 COUSINS
1 HERO = 70% of budget, owns 1 persona
1 FIGHTER = for trial
1 LIMITED = for hype

Discovery Set 5 x 2ml + Full-Size Voucher.
Blind test on TikTok Live. Spray cards up to 500 micro-KOCs.
My KPI: 30% Discovery → Full Size in 14 days.
If not hit, your story is wrong, not your ad.

4. OWN TROPICAL + HALAL + LAYERING
Buyer asks in 5 seconds: Is it Halal? Will it last in Jakarta heat? Can I layer it?
Show 8-hour wear test + Halal cert upfront. Trust > Hype.

5. PROTECT YOUR HERO PRICE
Discovery Set = Entry. 30ml = Gift. 50ml = HERO, margin driver. 100ml = Premium.
Never discount the Hero. Discount the entry.

6. DIFFERENT JOBS PER CHANNEL, SAME PRICE
Marketplace & TikTok Shop = Trial
Beauty Store & Retail Store = Trust, Tester, Experience
Website = Loyalty, Refill, Member-Only

7. DROP, DON'T LAUNCH
500 pcs limited, numbered, early access.
Then let UGC sell: Scent Personality Quiz, Spray & React, and Rate My Perfume.

MY FORMULA:
Perfume = Trust x Memory x Trial

No Memory = Forgotten
No Trial = No Trust
No Trust = No Repeat

The leaders of the US, China and Russia sat at one table in Shenzhen this week.

Their joint declaration has four points. I doubt any of them will change how you run your Asia business next year.

Three quieter decisions from the same week will.

1️⃣ASEAN signed its digital rulebook. On 14 November, the 11 member states of ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations) signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement. It is the first region-wide deal of its kind, with common rules on cross-border data flows, digital payments, digital identity and AI. ASEAN estimates it could help the region's digital economy reach US$2 trillion by 2030.

2️⃣Singapore takes the ASEAN chair on 1 January. Its theme is "Deeper Integration, Wider Partnerships", with priorities in finance, digital and energy. 2027 is also ASEAN's 60th anniversary. If you are deciding where to base your regional headquarters, this matters. Next year, the region's agenda will be set from here.

3️⃣Washington drew a new line through Southeast Asia. Under a rule announced on 16 November, exporting advanced AI chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia now requires a US licence. The goal is to stop Chinese developers from renting computing power in the region's data centres. Singapore says it is studying the details.

I see the same pattern every time.

Great-power summits make the headlines. The regulatory detail creates the work: who you can sell to, where your data can sit, and which entity signs the contract.
Meanwhile, the US-China trade truce still expires on 10 January.

If your 2027 Asia plan was written before this week, take another look at it. At Meridium, we work through these questions with companies before they set up, not after.

China Added 318 GW of Solar in Just ONE Year. Indonesia Targets 100 GWp.

But here's the real question: Are we ready to scale the infrastructure or just the ambition? Lets learned from China.

China's solar expansion is not simply a success story of cheaper panels. It reflects decades of strategic investment in manufacturing, transmission networks, energy storage, financing, and coordinated policy execution.

Indonesia's 100 GWp solar ambition presents an extraordinary opportunity. But replicating China's scale requires more than replicating its technology.

Five structural bottlenecks deserve our attention:

⚡ Grid Readiness — Can our fragmented power systems absorb massive solar capacity without compromising reliability?
🏭Supply Chain & Bankability — Can domestic manufacturing ambitions coexist with globally competitive financing requirements?
💰Financing & Risk Allocation — Who absorbs currency, off-taker, and investment risks to unlock private capital?
🌏Land & Spatial Planning — Can we secure suitable locations without creating new environmental and social challenges?
📑Regulatory & Market Certainty — Can our procurement and PPA frameworks move as fast as our deployment ambitions?

Perhaps we need to rethink how we measure success.
Not merely by how many GWp we install, but by how much electricity our grids can absorb, how much investment we can mobilize, and how much meaningful economic and social value we deliver.

Because the cheapest solar project is not necessarily the most valuable project for the power system.

And more importantly:
“COD is a milestone. Energy delivered is the impact.”

China offers a valuable benchmark. But Indonesia needs its own execution architecture—one that aligns grid readiness, bankable procurement, industrial development, and catalytic financing.

The next energy transition breakthrough may not come from building more solar panels. It may come from removing the structural barriers that prevent them from delivering value.

Article 6 Has a $71 Billion Carbon Credit Pipeline. Why Is Only $1.6 Billion Contracted?

At COP31, the Article 6 Network released its first State of the Article 6 Carbon Market 2026 report, revealing a striking imbalance between potential carbon credit supply and contracted demand. The report identifies approximately 2.36 billion tonnes of potential mitigation outcomes through 2030, representing an estimated $$70.9 billion in market value at an assumed price of $30 per tonne. Yet sovereign buyers have contracted only around 53 million tonnes, valued at approximately $1.6 billion. Despite 113 bilateral agreements between governments and 309 Article 6.2 activities being initiated, only about 151,566 tonnes of internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) have actually moved between countries. The figures highlight the considerable distance between establishing an international carbon trading framework and developing a functioning market with predictable transaction volumes.

What makes this particularly interesting from a financing perspective is the difference between potential credit generation and bankable carbon revenues. Project developers may have technically viable activities capable of generating substantial emissions reductions, but lenders and investors cannot necessarily underwrite projected credit volumes without credible buyers, agreed pricing, host-country authorization and clear delivery arrangements. According to the report, approximately 90% of planned Article 6.2 mitigation outcomes still lack an identified sovereign buyer. This creates a commercial bottleneck where project supply is developing faster than contracted demand. Recent transactions, including Norway's agreement to purchase up to 12 million credits from Indonesia, demonstrate that governments are beginning to move beyond bilateral cooperation frameworks toward actual purchase commitments. However, these agreements must still translate into verified issuance, corresponding adjustments, international transfers and ultimately payments to project developers.

The next phase of Article 6 may depend less on creating additional supply and more on converting the existing pipeline into financeable transactions. For host countries, this means establishing transparent authorization procedures, credible registries and predictable rules for sharing mitigation outcomes. For buyers, it requires long-term procurement commitments and sufficient confidence in credit integrity and delivery. For investors, the critical question is whether carbon purchase agreements can provide reliable enough cash flows to support project development and structured financing. The $71 billion figure illustrates the scale of potential market supply, but it should not be mistaken for committed investment or realizable revenue. The real measure of Article 6's success will be how much of that pipeline becomes contracted, financed, issued and transferred over the coming years.

Engineers study how things fail. At the Failure Modes of Engineering (FeME) Gathering inThe University of Edinburgh last month, we practiced studying how systems fail.
The idea that stuck with me: a commons is an engineered system, try reading Elinor Ostrom’s eight design principles in reverse, and each one becomes a failure mode. You ask how it breaks, why the principle went missing, what happens to the resource and the people, and what the "first warning" sign is.
 
Two examples we worked with:
 → A flood defence protects one street and pushes water onto the next. The boundary was drawn around a street or administrative boundaries for financial access, not the catchment. First warning sign: water pooling just beyond the new wall after ordinary rain.
 → A culvert nobody checks until it floods. Inspection isn’t anyone’s job. First warning sign: water ponding upstream after moderate rain.
 
Tools I’m taking home:
1. Co-creation as shared ownership of risk. If you want to go far, go with company.
2. Causal mapping: short statements, action verbs, and “why?” and “how?” to ladder up and down
3. Stakeholder mapping: gatekeepers, decision powers, vested interests, and where interests overlap
4. Critical systems heuristics: who is the client, who decides, who is the expert, and who speaks for those affected but not in the room, including future generations and nature
 
Reflecting on our own work:  I presented our Jakarta compound flood study withDwiva Anbiya Taruna through the participatory GIShttps://theamreta.com platform targeting Penjaringan, Cilincing, and Gelora. 88% of surveyed households have direct flood experience, and 62%+ face flooding 2–3 times a year. Recovery takes under a week, but households pay for it out of pocket. In residential areas, women lead pooled neighbourhood funds to run pumps, this means that savings need to be reflected in climate change and disaster resilience. These efforts happen while parts of the community, such as children and elders, rarely get to speak at sub-district meetings.
 
Through the Ostrom lens, communities already run local rules that work. The weak points may be where those rules meet the larger system: who recognises them, who funds drainage, and who hears the quieter voices. That is my reading to test with communities, not a conclusion.
 
What’s next:
 
1. Take the results back to the districts, validate them, and close the loop
2. Build causal and stakeholder maps together with gatekeepers
3. Name our project’s failure mode and its first warning sign
4. Scope how this becomes an actionable proposal with partners and affected communities
 
What is the first warning sign of failure in a system you work on?
